title: The Mexica Foundation Omen
subtitle: An origin tradition for the city of Mexico

learningObjectives.text: What omen do the nomadic Nahua see in Spence's account?

omen.author: Lewis Spence
omen.locator: Chapter I · THE CIVILISATION OF MEXICO; Chapter I · THE CIVILISATION OF MEXICO, normalized characters 46465-47015
omen.excerpt: The most popular of these relates how the nomadic Nahua beheld perched upon a cactus plant an eagle of great size and majesty, grasping in its talons a huge serpent, and spreading its wings to catch the rays of the rising sun. The soothsayers or medicine-men of the tribe, reading a good omen in the spectacle, advised the leaders of the people to settle on the spot, and, hearkening to the voice of what they considered divine authority, they proceeded to drive piles into the marshy ground, and thus laid the foundation of the great city of Mexico.
omen.note: Verbatim prose from Lewis Spence's early twentieth-century synthesis, not a direct translation of the Indigenous source material he discusses. Preserve its dated, colonial framing.

narrativeBlocks.title: A sign at a marshy site
narrativeBlocks.body: Spence recounts a migration legend in which the Nahua see an eagle on a cactus with a serpent in its talons and the rising sun behind it.

narrativeBlocks.title: Reading the sign
narrativeBlocks.body: Quotation from Spence's English prose synthesis (whitespace normalized): “The most popular of these relates how the nomadic Nahua beheld perched upon a cactus plant an eagle of great size and majesty, grasping in its talons a huge serpent, and spreading its wings to catch the rays of the rising sun. The soothsayers or medicine-men of the tribe, reading a good omen in the spectacle, advised the leaders of the people to settle on the spot, and, hearkening to the voice of what they considered divine authority, they proceeded to drive piles into the marshy ground, and thus laid the foundation of the great city of Mexico.”

narrativeBlocks.title: A settlement follows
narrativeBlocks.body: In Spence's account, interpreters read the sight as a good omen and advise the people to settle there; they begin building on the marshy ground.

narrativeBlocks.title: An origin narrative is not a site report
narrativeBlocks.body: Spence presents this as a popular legend about the foundation of Mexico. It is evidence for the written origin account, not independent proof that the event happened as described.

narrativeBlocks.title: Name the people and source
narrativeBlocks.body: The passage concerns the Mexica/Nahua migration story as Spence records it; it should not be made representative of all Mesoamerican histories.
